name: Yusuf Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's our family farm, up the valley above the town. Ninety beef cows, about two hundred ewes, hay and a bit of oats for the cattle. My father's 63 and stepping back, so I run the stock and the day-to-day, and my younger brother Sami does the machinery. I'm out at first light, feed round, check the cows, and I'm in for evening prayers if the work allows.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's ours. My grandfather bought this ground one field at a time, and every wall on it, somebody in my family built or fixed. What grinds me down is the forms and the inspections. Every year there's a new rule from people who've never had muck on their boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. It's all talk from people who sell things. I'd say it at the market on Thursday and we'd all have a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes here, which suits me. I don't use it, never have. My brother would be disappointed, he's always reading about gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. We're putting the new cattle shed up next year, the bank's agreed it. Calving in spring, lambing after. Same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sami say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep buying his gadgets, and I'd keep telling him not to. We have this argument every winter. Sami would buy a robot to open a gate if I let him, and I'd still walk over and open it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the real worry on the farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, weather, and whether the young ones will want to farm. That's always been the question round here. Not robots.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, because it was all talk from people who sell things. I'd say it at Thursday's livestock market and we'd all have a laugh.
S0.think: I think nothing changes here, which suits me, since I've never used these tools. My younger brother would be disappointed because he loves gadgets.
S0.do: Carries on with the usual year, with the bank-funded cattle shed going up next year, calving in spring and lambing after. Changes nothing about how the farm runs.
S0.quote: Sami would buy a robot to open a gate if I let him, and I'd still walk over and open it myself.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf's identity is rooted in family land his grandfather built up field by field. His gentle rivalry with his gadget-loving brother Sami runs through his answers. The farm's true worries in his eyes are prices, weather and the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have always worked hard and we don't need anyone's handouts, robots or no robots. If you're good at your job, you'll be fine. I'd say that at the mosque and at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the big farms down in the flat land would get robots first and their beef would get cheaper. Then our price goes down. That's how it goes, I'm not complaining, but it would squeeze us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big at first. I'd wait to see whether the prices actually move. If Sami wanted to try something, I'd let him try it on the hay, as long as he paid for it out of his own pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cow that won't settle before calving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not complaining. But isn't that unfair on farms like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But that's the market. If they do it cheaper, they've earned it. I don't want the government stopping them, I want them to be better at it than us, if they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got tight, what would you fall back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father's built up a bit, and the land is the land. We wouldn't go hungry. But I've only got a few months of my own money put by, so I'd be careful.

S1.say: I'd say farmers have always worked hard and we don't need anyone's handouts, robots or not. If you're good at your job you'll be fine, and I'd say that at the mosque and the market.
S1.think: I think the big lowland farms would get robots first, their beef would get cheaper and our price would be squeezed. That's the market, but it would hurt.
S1.do: Waits to see whether prices really move before changing anything. Lets his brother try a machine on the hay if he pays for it himself.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cow that won't settle before calving.
S1.quote: I don't want the government stopping them, I want them to be better at it than us, if they can.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf accepts market competition even when it hurts his own farm, which fits his free-market views. He leans on the family's land and his father's savings rather than any government. He'd let his brother experiment, but only with his own money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right, it's too quick, and the people selling this will be the only ones who win. I'd say families like ours built this country. I'm not one for protests, but I'd say it plainly to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd lose money every year until we couldn't. The big farms would run robots day and night and sell beef for half. We've got the bank loan on the shed. That keeps me up just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the shed if we hadn't started, and if we had I'd cut everything else. No new truck, no holiday, I'd sell some of the young stock early to pay down the loan. I'd ask the family and our community to help each other with labour so nobody's paying wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, would you change how you farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Two years isn't enough to learn something new, and I'm not going to be good at it anyway. I'd rather be poor on my own ground than comfortable in a job watching screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father. He's given his whole life to this. Seeing it go in two years, at his age, would break him. I'd have to tell him, and I don't know how.

S2.say: I'd say it's too quick and that only the people selling the technology will win. Families like ours built this country, and I'd say that plainly to anyone, though I wouldn't protest.
S2.think: I think we'd lose money every year until we couldn't go on, because big farms would sell beef for half the price. With a bank loan on the new shed, that thought keeps me up.
S2.do: Cuts all extra spending, sells some young stock early to pay down the shed loan and drops any new purchases. Asks family and the local community to share labour so nobody pays wages.
S2.feel: Alarmed and properly frightened, especially for his father.
S2.quote: I'd rather be poor on my own ground than comfortable in a job watching screens.
S2.fieldNote: Yusuf's fear is financial and personal: a bank loan and a father who has given his life to the farm. He rejects retraining outright and would rather be poor on his own land. His answer to hardship is family and community sharing, not government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but slower. Families and communities need to stick together. I'd tell younger farmers to pay off debt, not take on more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us time to pay down the loan, at least. I'd still lose in the end on price, I think. But I'd be able to look my father in the eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the shed loan off as fast as I could, maybe three years instead of eight. I'd cut back on everything that isn't the farm. And I'd talk to our neighbours about sharing machinery and labour, like the old days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Still frightened, but there's a bit of ground under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sami say to that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, use the robots, idiot. And maybe he's right for the hay. I'll let Sami put a robot in the hay field, but nobody puts a robot in my calving shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between five years and two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd be fighting to keep the farm. Five years, I'd be fighting to keep it the way it is. That's different.

S3.say: I'd say families and communities need to stick together, and younger farmers should pay off debt instead of taking more on. It's the same message as before, just with a bit more time.
S3.think: I think five years gives us time to pay down the loan, though we'd likely still lose on price in the end. At least I'd be able to look my father in the eye.
S3.do: Pays off the shed loan in about three years instead of eight and cuts spending that isn't for the farm. Talks to neighbours about sharing machinery and labour, as farms used to.
S3.feel: Anxious and still frightened, but with some ground under his feet.
S3.quote: I'll let Sami put a robot in the hay field, but nobody puts a robot in my calving shed.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Yusuf's focus shifts from saving the farm to keeping it as it is. He'd allow his brother's robots in the hay field but draws a hard line at the calving shed. Paying off debt is his main defence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot of what they promise won't happen. I'd say it at the market. And I'd say farming families will still be here after the companies go bust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm 37 and the farm is probably mine by then. I'd want to get married and have children before then, so they know the farm the way I did. That's more important to me than any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep farming, pay the loan off, save something each year. I'd look for a wife, if I'm honest, my mother's been telling me for years. And I'd let Sami try his machines, slowly, with his own money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It doesn't go away, it just gets quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the farm survives to 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the farm keeps going in some way, even if it's smaller. Land is land. If the robots grow everything, people will still want to know a man who raised his own beef.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse to do, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning it myself. I won't. Sami can. Maybe that's how it should be, one brother keeps the old ways and one learns the new.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is long and a lot of what's promised won't happen. Farming families will still be here after the companies go bust, and I'd say that at the market.
S4.think: I think the farm will probably be mine by 37, and I'd want a wife and children before then so they know the farm as I did. That matters more to me than any machine.
S4.do: Keeps farming, pays off the loan and saves something each year. Looks to marry and start a family, and lets his brother try new machines slowly with his own money.
S4.feel: Anxious; the worry doesn't leave, it just gets quieter.
S4.quote: If the robots grow everything, people will still want to know a man who raised his own beef.
S4.fieldNote: The long runway brings Yusuf's family plans to the front: marriage, children and handing on the land. He still won't learn the technology himself but accepts a split between the brothers. His hope rests on people valuing beef raised by a family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, with the loan on the shed. What would help isn't handouts. It'd be fair prices for family farms, a bank that gives us time on the loan, and labels so people know who raised their food.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It matters. When the robots come, I'll still be at Friday prayers, and the man next to me will still need help with his hay.

headlineQuote: When the robots come, I'll still be at Friday prayers, and the man next to me will still need help with his hay.
portrait: Yusuf Diaz, 27, runs the stock and day-to-day on his family's hill farm with his father, who is stepping back, and his gadget-loving brother Sami. He never uses AI tools, distrusts people who sell technology and believes in markets, family and faith over handouts. A fizzling AI pleases him and steady change makes him uneasy about prices. The two-year picture alarms him because of the bank loan on a new shed and his father's life's work, while more time lets him pay down debt and plan to marry and raise children on the farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because cheap robot-raised beef and the loan on the new shed could sink the family farm.
whatWouldHelp: Fair prices for family farms, more time from the bank on the loan and labels showing who raised the food, rather than handouts.
